clue.text: Author of decision about 1,500 feet going to sleep

indicators.note: the decision is placed about, that is surrounding, the measurement and the sleep that follow it

parts.note: a ruling is a decision, as by a judge
a yard is three feet, so 1,500 feet is 500 yards: D, the Roman 500, plus YARD
kip is British slang for a sleep

explanation.surface: A writer's verdict on a long stretch of ground that sends someone to sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: '1,500 feet' looks like a number to translate whole; it splits into the Roman numeral for 500 and a unit of three feet, since 500 yards make 1,500 feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling wrote The Jungle Book and Kim, so he is a famous English writer of stories and poems.

clue.text: Worker constrained by gout, sadly, amid thunderous noise of fighting

indicators.note: the worker is held in, hemmed by the letters of the ailment around it
amid puts the whole assembly in the middle of the loud noise that follows

parts.note: thunder rumbles

indicators.note: things that go sadly go wrong, so the ailment's letters fall into a different order

parts.note: the painful joint ailment, taken as written for rearranging
a hand is a manual worker, as in farmhand

explanation.surface: A labourer suffering from gout, caught up in the din of a brawl.
explanation.walkthrough: Two containers nest: the worker sits inside the shuffled ailment, and that string sits inside the noise, after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Rough-and-tumble describes disorderly, haphazard scuffling, a scrap or tussle without rules, so it stands for fighting.

clue.text: French philosopher: 'is decay is queried

parts.note: turning a statement into a question puts 'did' at its front: did it rot?
the apostrophe drops the H of his, so the matching dropped-H pronoun is 'e, he
rot is decay

explanation.surface: A cockney asking whether something of his has gone rotten.
explanation.walkthrough: ''Is decay' asked as a question, in the same dropped-H voice, becomes 'Did 'e rot?', which runs together as DIDEROT.
explanation.definitionFit: Denis Diderot was the eighteenth-century French thinker who edited the Encyclopédie during the Enlightenment.

clue.text: Hormone that's red in Lana Turner

indicators.note: a turner turns things round, so the words before it are spun into a new order

parts.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A hormone that makes the film star Lana Turner blush.
explanation.walkthrough: Lana Turner looks like one name, the Hollywood actress; the surname is the signal working on 'red in Lana'.
explanation.definitionFit: Adrenalin is the chemical messenger released by the adrenal glands under stress, a classic example of a hormone.

clue.text: Entrance by party or style

parts.note: a do is an informal word for a party
taken as written
a way of doing something is its style or manner

explanation.surface: Choosing whether to come in by the party route or the stylish route.
explanation.definitionFit: A doorway is the opening in a wall through which one goes in, so it is a way of entry.

clue.text: In radio no mercy is shown to constituent of bottle

indicators.note: the answer is found in the run of words that follows, spanning their boundaries
the letters are on show already in the phrase, simply waiting to be read off

parts.note: read straight through, spanning the three words

explanation.surface: A merciless radio broadcast, oddly tied to what a bottle is made of.
explanation.definitionFit: An ionomer is a type of tough plastic polymer used in packaging, so it can be a material that bottles are made from.

clue.text: Actress exchanging role with Pole

indicators.note: exchanging places swaps letters around, so the part's letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written for rearranging
N, the north pole, is a standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A performer swapping parts with a Polish co-star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' looks like a Polish person; it is a magnetic pole, N.
explanation.definitionFit: Sophia Loren is the Italian film star of the 1950s and 60s, an Oscar-winning screen performer.

clue.text: No sense in it? No, none: her merry heart is broken

indicators.note: a broken thing is in pieces, and the pieces are put back together differently

parts.words: No, none: her merry heart is
parts.note: all the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone protests that nothing makes sense, since her happy heart has been shattered.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition stops at the question mark; 'No' after it begins the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'neither rhyme nor reason' describes something lacking any logic or sense at all.

clue.text: See 7
Suffer German and consequently Latin

parts.note: und is the German word for and
ergo is Latin for therefore, consequently

explanation.surface: Someone enduring German, and therefore Latin too, as school lessons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'German' and 'Latin' look like subjects; each tells you which language to translate the neighbouring word into.
explanation.definitionFit: To undergo an operation or ordeal is to experience or endure it, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Destination of selenite and not heartless magician

indicators.note: without a heart, the word loses its central letter

parts.note: nor means and not; the 'and' before it is absorbed
a witch works magic

explanation.surface: A puzzling destination for a moon-dweller, set against a magician without a heart.
explanation.walkthrough: A selenite is an inhabitant of the moon. In the nursery rhyme, the Man in the Moon came down too soon and asked his way to Norwich, a city in eastern England.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyme names that East Anglian city as where the lunar visitor was heading, so it is his journey's end.

clue.text: Proceeding after ladybird

indicators.note: after puts the first-named piece second, behind the lady who follows it in the clue

parts.note: a lady is referred to as her
to be on is to be under way, proceeding

explanation.surface: A ladybird crawling along behind something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ladybird' looks like the beetle, but it splits: 'lady' is wordplay and 'bird' the definition. 'After' places the second piece behind the first.
explanation.definitionFit: The heron is a long-legged wading fowl of rivers and marshes, so it is a kind of bird.

clue.text: Dr Lewis's round near 10

indicators.note: one name goes round the other, enclosing the doctor's title

parts.note: Wyndham Lewis was the English painter and writer; his first name is taken
MO, medical officer, is a doctor

explanation.surface: A doctor called Lewis doing his rounds near some place.
explanation.walkthrough: Dr Lewis looks like a person's name and title; 'Lewis's' is Wyndham Lewis, whose first name goes round MO. Wymondham is a market town in Norfolk, pronounced 'Windum'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norfolk town lies a few miles south-west of the city at 10 across, so it is close by.

clue.text: Catcher and actor, a smasher?

parts.note: a net catches fish or butterflies
a player is an actor on the stage

explanation.surface: A cricketer who catches and also acts, a real smasher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smasher' sounds like praise for someone gorgeous; in tennis, a smash is a hard overhead shot, often hit near the net.
explanation.definitionFit: A tennis volleyer who rushes forward to the net often finishes points with smashes, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Mathematician didn't finish in Italy

definitions.note: the answer is a place in Italy, not a phrase

indicators.note: something not finished stops short, so the name loses its last letter

parts.note: Alan Turing, the British codebreaker and computing pioneer

explanation.surface: A mathematician who left his work incomplete while in Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: Turin is the north Italian city in Piedmont, famous for its shroud and Fiat, so it is found within that country.

clue.text: Ornamental inveiglements?

parts.note: surface reading: decorative adornments, the finery of a ceremonial outfit
setter's reading: acts of luring someone into a snare, read off the word itself

explanation.walkthrough: The answer means decorations, but read as a verb it also means catching in snares, which is what inveiglements are; the question mark flags the play.
explanation.definitionFit: Trappings are outward ornaments and accessories, while trapping someone is luring them, so both halves fit.

clue.text: Shakespearean part of a sanctimonious nature

definitions.note: adjective for a noun answer: a Shakespearean character

indicators.note: only a portion of the following word is taken, the letters sitting inside it

parts.note: read from inside the long adjective

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare role played in a self-righteous way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part' looks like a theatre role; here it signals letters taken from inside a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Timon of Athens is the title character of one of the Bard's tragedies, a misanthropic Greek nobleman.

clue.text: Mummy's girl going round in charge of spelling?

parts.note: ma is a child's word for mother, like mummy

indicators.note: the girl goes round, enclosing the abbreviation that follows

parts.note: gal is an informal word for a girl
IC is the standard abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: A mother's daughter who supervises the class spelling lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spelling' looks like writing words letter by letter; here it means casting spells, and the question mark flags the play.
explanation.definitionFit: Magical describes anything to do with spells and sorcery, so it is an adjective meaning relating to enchantments.

clue.text: Steam train carrying a divine serpent

indicators.note: a train that carries something holds it inside

parts.note: puffer, or puffer train, is a child's name for a steam train
taken as written
DD, Doctor of Divinity, stands for a divine, a clergyman

explanation.surface: A steam train transporting a clergyman and a snake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divine' looks like an adjective; it is a noun, a clergyman, abbreviated DD.
explanation.definitionFit: The puff adder is a venomous African viper that inflates itself when threatened, so it is a kind of snake.

clue.text: How much, including tax if Anne is involved, for initiative?

definitions.note: the answer is the phrase that precedes 'Initiative' in the name PFI

indicators.note: the cost includes, so holds inside, everything that comes after it

parts.note: the price is how much something costs
VAT, value added tax, is the British sales tax

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so the name and the word before it are jumbled

parts.note: the letters taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: Asking the cost, tax included, if Anne is part of a business venture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'If' looks like a link word but does double duty as part of the jumbled letters. PFI, the Private Finance Initiative, was a British public-funding scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: The Private Finance Initiative was the UK government scheme funding public projects with private money, so these two words complete its title.

clue.text: See 17 Down
Has a second function when tramlines are in use

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a thing that also serves as something else ... as it
second meaning: the tennis game for pairs, when the outer side strips of the court count

explanation.walkthrough: Tramlines are the narrow side strips of a tennis court, in play only for the four-player game. 'Tramlines' tempts toward trams and transport.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means serves a dual purpose, and the noun is the tennis format played two against two using the full width.

clue.text: Russian aircraft with share of international travel?

parts.note: the MiG is a Russian fighter jet
a ration is a fixed share or allowance

explanation.surface: Russian jets each taking a portion of global air traffic.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark signals a loose definition: birds and peoples cross borders when they move seasonally or resettle.
explanation.definitionFit: Birds and peoples often journey from one country to another when moving seasonally or resettling, which is this movement.

clue.text: Bill keeps a day for the poet's continent

indicators.note: the bill keeps, so holds within itself, the day that follows

parts.note: AC, account, is a bill
Fri is the abbreviation for Friday, a day of the week

explanation.surface: An invoice held back for a day before it reaches the poet's homeland.
explanation.definitionFit: Afric is an old poetic form of Africa, used in verse, hence the reference to a poet's way of naming the landmass.

clue.text: Stop listening to the catwalk operators

indicators.note: listening means taking the word by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: what a cat walks on is its paws

explanation.surface: Halting to hear the people who run a fashion show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catwalk' looks like a fashion runway; read literally, it is a cat walking, and paws do the work.
explanation.definitionFit: A pause is a brief halt or break, and to pause is to stop for a moment, so the words match.

clue.text: Put in liquor, confused rat with lizard

parts.note: to lace a drink is to add spirits to it

indicators.note: a confused animal is muddled, so its letters come in a muddled order

parts.note: taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: A drunken, bewildered rat dropped into liquor along with a lizard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put in liquor' looks like soaking something in drink; here it means adding drink to something.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacerta is the genus of green and wall lizards, and its Latin name means lizard.

clue.text: Baffle in France no longer

parts.note: non is French for no
plus is French for more, as in no more, no longer

explanation.surface: Someone no longer able to bewilder people while living in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In France' says to translate the words that follow: non plus, French for 'no more', a state of being unable to go further.
explanation.definitionFit: To nonplus someone is to perplex them so they do not know what to say or do, so it means to bewilder.

clue.text: Maid in bed, servant likewise, with Poles around America

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another; likewise says the servant is placed the same way

parts.note: taken as written
a lackey is a footman or servant

indicators.note: the two poles stand on either side, around the country

parts.note: S and N, the south and north poles
the abbreviation for the United States

explanation.surface: A housemaid in bed, a manservant too, with Polish visitors gathered around an American.
explanation.walkthrough: Black-eyed Susan is the heroine of John Gay's ballad, a girl parting from her sailor Sweet William. 'Likewise' tells you the servant also goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: In the old ballad she is the young woman bidding farewell to her sweetheart, so she is a maiden.
